## Lithosphere and plate motion
Let's start with a quick check. From memory: what layer do the plates float on? Try to answer before reading on.
The lithosphere is Earth's hard outer shell. It is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates. A mosaic means many pieces fitted together, like tiles. The plates float on the asthenosphere. That is a ductile layer, meaning soft and able to flow slowly.
Words and a picture: Lithosphere = rigid plates Asthenosphere = soft, flowing layer plates | plates | plates --------|--------|-------- ~~~~ asthenosphere (flows) ~~~~
Why do plates move? Three drivers: mantle convection (slow churning of hot rock), slab pull (a sinking plate edge pulls the rest), and ridge push (new rock at a ridge pushes plates apart).
How fast? Relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹). That is about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Plates meet at boundaries. Three types: Divergent → pull apart → normal faults, shallow Convergent → collide → thrust faults, deep to shallow Transform → slide past → strike-slip, shallow to intermediate
Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries? Plate edges are locked by friction. Strain builds until it exceeds rock strength, then it snaps loose. That snap is the quake.
Other clustering causes: old faults concentrate slip. Cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, so deformation focuses there. Curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Key point, in different words: quakes are not scattered by chance. They trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. Kinematic means about motion. Where plates move, quakes follow.
Tomorrow, recall this one line: earthquakes trace plate interactions, not chance.
Key: Earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions.
Key: The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere.
Key: Relative motion is measured in centimetres per year.
Key: Plate edges lock by friction; strain builds until it exceeds rock strength.

Q: How fast do plates move relative to each other? A: Centimetres per year. The material says relative motion is measured in centimetres per year.
Q: At a divergent boundary, plates do what? A: Pull apart. Divergent means plates pull apart.
Q: Which fault type marks a transform boundary? Type it. A: strike-slip. Transform boundaries make strike-slip earthquakes.
Q: A quake is very deep. Which boundary fits best? A: Convergent. Convergent boundaries give thrust-fault quakes, deep to shallow.
Q: Name one of the three drivers of plate motion. A: mantle convection (or slab pull, or ridge push). Mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push move the plates.

## Types of plate boundaries

Divergent: plates pull apart. Convergent: plates collide. Transform: plates slide past each other.
Each motion makes its own earthquake type. Pull apart makes normal-fault quakes, shallow. Colliding makes thrust-fault quakes, deep to shallow. Sliding past makes strike-slip quakes, shallow to intermediate.

## Why earthquakes cluster at boundaries

Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries? Plate edges are locked by friction. Strain builds up until it is stronger than the rock. Then it snaps: an earthquake.
Three more reasons: old faults focus the slip. Cold, brittle rock sits next to warm, soft rock, so bending happens there. Curved plate edges force shear into narrow zones.
Wrong idea to drop: earthquakes are random. They are not. They trace the kinematic framework, the pattern of how plates move. Same idea in other words: quake maps are plate-motion maps.

## Plate speeds and the Ring of Fire
Plates move slowly, but fast plates make big earthquakes often.
The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm each year. It slides past North America.
The Nazca Plate dives under South America at about 8 cm each year. Diving under is called subduction.
Fast motion like this explains why the Ring of Fire has many large earthquakes.
Deep quakes happen in subducting slabs, 30–300 km down. Shallow quakes happen at ridges and transform faults.
Between quakes, the locked zone stores strain. Then slip releases it in seconds. This is the seismic cycle.
A gap is a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle. Gaps are candidates for future large events.

## Earthquake depth distribution
Quick check first: where do most deep earthquakes happen? Try to answer from memory before reading on.
Earthquakes come at different depths. Shallow ones are 10 km deep or less. Deep ones are 30 to 300 km deep.
Shallow quakes happen at ridges (plates pull apart) and transform faults (plates slide past). Deep quakes happen where one plate sinks under another. That sinking zone is called the Wadati-Benioff zone.
Deep quakes get energy from two things: the crust bending, and the slab losing water (dehydration).
Here is the depth map in one picture: Ridges / transform faults → shallow (≤ 10 km) Subducting slab → deep (30–300 km) Key idea: depth tells you the plate setting.
A seismic gap is a fault segment that has not broken in a full earthquake cycle. Gaps are places where a big quake may happen next.
The seismic cycle has steps: strain builds up (interseismic), slip happens fast (coseismic), then stress moves around (postseismic).
Key point in other words: if a fault part has been quiet for a whole cycle, it may be storing up a large quake.

## Seismic cycle at a convergent margin
Let's learn the seismic cycle. That is the pattern of an earthquake area over time. Try to recall: what happens first, before a big quake?
The cycle has four steps. First is interseismic. The locked zone stores strain for decades or centuries. Strain means stored pushing force.
Second is coseismic. Slip happens fast. Stored elastic energy is released in seconds to minutes.
Third is postseismic. Afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation move stress around. This takes months to years. Afterslip is slow slip after the quake. Viscoelastic relaxation means deep rock slowly flows and eases stress.
Fourth is preseismic. Some quakes give warning signs first. These are foreshocks and slow slip.
Here is the cycle as a chain: interseismic (strain builds) → coseismic (slip) → postseismic (stress moves) → back to interseismic
Fast plates make more big quakes. The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm per year. The Nazca Plate goes under South America at about 8 cm per year. This is why the Ring of Fire has many large quakes.
Depth tells us the plate setting. Shallow quakes (10 km or less) happen at ridges and transform faults. Deeper quakes (30–300 km) happen in the Wadati-Benioff zone of a sinking slab.
Seismic gap theory says: a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle may be due for a big event. GPS and InSAR measure plate speeds in cm per year to check how locked the zone is.
One point to recall tomorrow: the four cycle steps are interseismic, coseismic, postseismic, preseismic.

## Seismic gap theory
Let's try a quick check first. What happens to a fault between big earthquakes? Type your guess.
Here is the idea. A fault can stay locked for a long time. During that time, strain builds up. Strain means stored pushing force in the rock.
The seismic cycle has steps. Interseismic: strain builds (decades to centuries). Coseismic: sudden slip, energy released (seconds to minutes). Postseismic: afterslip and slow relaxation (months to years).
Picture it as a chain: locked zone → strain builds → sudden slip → stress moves → locked again
Now the main point. Seismic gap theory says: a fault segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle is a candidate for a future large event. Rupture means the fault breaks and slips.
A gap is not a safe place. It is a place where strain has had time to build. That is why gaps matter for hazard assessment.
Wrong idea to avoid: 'no earthquakes lately means it is safe.' It fails because the strain is still stored. The right view: a quiet segment may be due for a big one.
Plate speeds help explain this. The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm per year. The Nazca Plate subducts (pushes under) South America at about 8 cm per year. Fast motion means strain builds fast.
GPS and InSAR measure these plate speeds. They help refine coupling models. Coupling means how tightly the plates are locked.
Tomorrow, recall this one line: a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle is a candidate for a future large event.
Key: Seismic gap theory: segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events.

Q: A fault segment has been quiet for a very long time. What does gap theory say? A: Strain has built, so a large event is possible. A long-quiet segment has not ruptured in a full cycle, so strain has built.
Q: Which cycle step releases stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes? A: Coseismic. Coseismic is the sudden slip step of the seismic cycle.
Q: Which tools monitor plate speeds to refine coupling models? A: GPS and InSAR. GPS and InSAR measure plate-scale velocities in cm per year.

## GPS and InSAR monitoring
Quick check first: what does GPS measure at plate scale? Try to recall before reading. Answer: speed in cm per year.
First idea: plate speed. GPS and InSAR measure how plates move. Speeds are small, in cm per year. Example: the Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm/yr past North America.
Second idea: earthquake depth. Shallow quakes (10 km or less) happen at ridges and transform faults. Deep quakes (30–300 km) happen in subducting slabs. Depth tells us how thick the risky zone is.
Third idea: the seismic cycle. Strain builds while the fault is locked. Then it slips fast in a big quake. Then afterslip follows for months to years.
Fourth idea: seismic gaps. A segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle may break next. This helps judge hazard.
Picture of the cycle: locked zone → strain builds (years) → sudden slip (seconds) → afterslip (months) → maybe foreshocks before
Key words defined: coupling = how tightly plates stick before they slip. Seismogenic = the depth range where quakes can start. InSAR = radar from space that measures ground motion.
Tomorrow, recall one line: GPS gives plate speed in cm/yr; quake depth shows how deep a rupture can go.

Key: Obtain relative plate velocities (cm yr⁻¹) from global models (e.g., MORVEL, NUVEL‑1A).
Key: Map earthquake depths (km) to infer the seismogenic thickness.
Key: Evaluate coupling and seismic gap status for probabilistic hazard.

## Hazard assessment workflow
Let's build a hazard check, step by step. Four steps. One idea each.
Step 1: Find the plate boundary type. Is it a subduction zone, a ridge, or a transform? Look at the region first.
Step 2: Get the plate speed. Use a global model like MORVEL or NUVEL-1A. Speed is in cm per year.
Step 3: Map how deep earthquakes are. Depth is in km. Deep and shallow quakes tell you the seismogenic thickness. That means the layer that can break in quakes.
Step 4: Check coupling and seismic gaps. Coupling means plates stick and store stress. A gap is a stretch with no recent big quake. Both feed a probabilistic hazard estimate.
Quick check: which step comes first? Yes — boundary type. Speed comes after.

Why depth matters: the depth spread shows how far a rupture could reach, and hints at tsunami risk.

Key: Obtain relative plate velocities (cm yr⁻¹) from global models (e.g., MORVEL, NUVEL-1A).

## Lithosphere and Tectonic Plates
The lithosphere is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates that float on the ductile asthenosphere. Think of it like a marching band's drill blocks: each block is rigid and moves as a unit, while the dancers between blocks shift fluidly like the asthenosphere. Plates move because of mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, and their relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
Boundary type controls seismic style. Divergent boundaries pull plates apart, producing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries collide plates, producing thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. Transform boundaries slide plates past each other, producing strike-slip earthquakes at shallow to intermediate depths.
Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries? Stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, and strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Think of it like a beekeeping hive frame held shut by a stiff latch: pressure builds until the latch gives suddenly. Fault geometry means pre-existing faults concentrate slip, rheological contrast means cold brittle lithosphere borders warm ductile mantle and focuses deformation, and geometric incompatibility means curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
The key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. Worked example: a transform boundary slides plates past each other, so expect strike-slip earthquakes at shallow to intermediate depths. Now you finish one: a convergent boundary collides plates, so the expected seismic style is thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. Last one, do it alone: a divergent boundary pulls plates apart, so predict the fault type and depth.
Key: Earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions.
Key: Divergent: plates pull apart; normal-fault earthquakes, shallow depths.
Key: The lithosphere is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates that float on the ductile asthenosphere.
Key: Relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
Key: Stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction; strain builds until it exceeds rock strength.

## The Seismic Cycle at a Convergent Margin
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has four stages. Interseismic: the locked zone accumulates strain over decades to centuries. Coseismic: sudden slip releases stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes. Postseismic: afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years. Preseismic: possible precursory signals like foreshocks and slow slip.
Think of it like a falconer's glove: the jess holds the bird's foot still (interseismic strain builds), then the grip releases in an instant (coseismic slip), and the leather slowly relaxes back to shape (postseismic).
